raw_text:
Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) is a mechanical strategy to reduce thromboembolism in atrial fibrillation (AF). The rationale is anatomically compelling: in nonvalvular AF, most atrial thrombi arise in the left atrial appendage (LAA), a trabeculated cul-de-sac with variable morphology, reduced contractility, and prothrombotic stasis during AF [1,2]. Current guidelines position percutaneous LAAC mainly for patients with AF, elevated stroke risk, and a contraindication or strong aversion to long-term oral anticoagulation (OAC), while emphasizing shared decision-making and careful assessment of bleeding risk, competing mortality, and procedural risk [3,4].

The field began with the PLAATO device, which established the feasibility of transseptal LAA sealing in high-risk patients but was not commercially sustained [5,6]. The Watchman program provided the pivotal randomized evidence. In PROTECT AF, LAAC was noninferior to warfarin for the composite of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular death, but early procedural complications—especially pericardial effusion—were important [7]. Subsequent safety analyses and the Continued Access experience showed a learning curve, with lower complication rates as operator experience increased [8]. Longer PROTECT AF follow-up reinforced noninferiority, while PREVAIL improved procedural safety but did not meet one coprimary efficacy endpoint, partly because the warfarin arm had unexpectedly low event rates [9,10]. Patient-level and 5-year pooled analyses of PROTECT AF and PREVAIL suggested comparable stroke prevention, fewer hemorrhagic strokes, and less late nonprocedural major bleeding after LAAC, but with the trade-off of upfront procedural risk [11,12].

Real-world registries broadened the evidence to patients less suitable for anticoagulation. ASAP supported Watchman implantation without a warfarin transition in patients considered ineligible for warfarin [13]. EWOLUTION showed high implant success and relatively low observed stroke rates in a population with frequent OAC contraindications, although interpretation was limited by nonrandomized design and historical-risk comparisons [14,15]. In the United States, the NCDR LAAO Registry demonstrated large-scale uptake, older and comorbid patients, high procedural success, and low in-hospital stroke and mortality, while confirming pericardial effusion and major bleeding as key early hazards [16]. The Watchman FLX iteration improved deliverability, recapture, and seal; PINNACLE FLX reported high successful implantation and low early safety events [17].

Evidence for other devices is strongest for the Amplatzer Amulet. A prospective global observational study supported feasibility and early outcomes with the Amulet design [18]. In Amulet IDE, Amulet was noninferior to Watchman 2.5 for safety and effectiveness and superior for complete occlusion, but procedure-related complications were numerically higher, again highlighting the importance of device selection and experience [19]. SWISS-APERO, using systematic computed tomography follow-up, found broadly similar LAA patency between Amulet and Watchman/FLX strategies, with device-specific differences in residual leak and procedural events [20].

Randomized comparisons with contemporary direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) have become central. PRAGUE-17 randomized high-risk patients to LAAC versus DOACs and found noninferiority for a composite of ischemic, bleeding, and cardiovascular outcomes, with durable 4-year findings [21,22]. OPTION addressed the common post-ablation dilemma and found LAAC after AF ablation reduced nonprocedural major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding and was noninferior for death, stroke, or systemic embolism compared with continued OAC [23]. In 2026, CHAMPION-AF extended this question to broader OAC-eligible AF patients and reported LAAC noninferior to NOAC therapy for cardiovascular death, stroke, or systemic embolism and superior for nonprocedural bleeding [24]. Conversely, CLOSURE-AF, in very high-risk patients with both stroke and bleeding vulnerability, did not show noninferiority versus physician-directed medical therapy, underscoring that LAAC is not automatically preferable in all high-risk phenotypes [25].

Several unresolved issues shape contemporary practice. Device-related thrombus occurs in a minority but is associated with stroke and systemic embolism, necessitating follow-up imaging and individualized antithrombotic therapy [26]. Peridevice leak, once considered acceptable if ≤5 mm, appears clinically relevant when persistent at 1 year, raising the importance of optimal sizing, coaxial deployment, and surveillance [27]. Postimplant pharmacotherapy remains heterogeneous: registry data suggest dual antiplatelet therapy after Watchman FLX may be comparable to OAC-based regimens in selected patients [28], while the small ADALA randomized trial suggested low-dose apixaban may reduce early device-related thrombosis compared with dual antiplatelet therapy [29]. Epicardial suture approaches such as LARIAT avoid an endocardial implant but introduce pericardial-access risks and have less robust randomized evidence than endocardial occluders [30].

In summary, percutaneous LAAC has evolved from a niche alternative for patients unable to tolerate anticoagulation into an evidence-based option with expanding indications. Its value is greatest when the competing risks are explicit: lifelong OAC bleeding and adherence on one side, and procedural complications, device-related thrombus, leak, and short-term antithrombotic exposure on the other. Future priorities include head-to-head trials in well-defined phenotypes, standardized imaging definitions, and randomized postimplant antithrombotic strategies.
